lessons.title: Visual Inspection Criteria
lessons.body: Visual inspection is your first and cheapest quality check. Before you power up any board, look at it under good light. You need a bright, white light sourceâa 10W LED desk lamp works well. Hold the board at a 45-degree angle to catch reflections. Start with the big things: are all components present? Check against your bill of materials (BOM). Missing parts are common when you hand-place. Next, look for solder bridgesâtiny balls of solder connecting two pads that shouldn't touch. A bridge between pins on an IC can destroy the chip when you power up. Also check for cold solder joints: they look dull and grainy, not shiny and smooth. In Africa, humidity and dust can cause problems, so inspect for corrosion or dirt on pads. Use a magnifying glass (10x) to see fine details. For through-hole parts, check that the lead fills the hole and solder wets both sides. For surface-mount, look for tombstoningâwhere one end of a component lifts off the pad. Also check for component orientation: diodes and electrolytic capacitors have polarity. A reversed electrolytic capacitor can explode. Look for scratches on the board that expose copper. Any exposed copper will oxidize and cause intermittent faults. Write down every defect you find on a paper log with the board serial number. A simple rule: if you wouldn't buy it, don't ship it. In a small workshop in Nairobi or Lagos, you might inspect 20 boards a day. Train your eyes to spot these issues in under 30 seconds per board. Remember, fixing a defect now takes 2 minutes; fixing it after the customer complains takes 2 hours and loses trust.

lessons.title: Using Magnification and Lighting
lessons.body: Your naked eye can only see details down to about 0.1 mm. Solder joints on modern boards are often 0.2 mm wide, so you need magnification. A simple 10x jeweler's loupe costs about $5 and clips to your eye or a stand. For serious work, get a stereo microscope with 10x to 40x zoom. In Africa, you can find used stereo microscopes on Jumia or from university surplus for $100â$300. Lighting is just as important. Use a ring light or two flexible gooseneck LEDsâone from the left, one from the rightâto eliminate shadows. Shadows hide cracks and cold joints. For inspecting solder joints, use a technique called 'coaxial lighting': light comes from the same direction you look. This makes shiny solder look bright and dull solder look dark. A cheap alternative is a white LED flashlight held at a low angle. Also use a dark backgroundâblack mat or black paperâto increase contrast. For very fine pitch ICs (0.5 mm pitch), you need at least 20x magnification. Clean your lens with a microfiber cloth; dust looks like defects. Set up a dedicated inspection station: a table with a boom stand for the microscope, adjustable LED lights, and a grounded wrist strap to prevent ESD damage. In hot, humid climates, add a small fan to prevent fogging on lenses. Practice by inspecting a known-good board first to calibrate your eyes. Then inspect a board with intentional defects (create them yourself) to learn what to look for. With practice, you can inspect a 100-component board in 5 minutes using 10x magnification and proper lighting. Without it, you'll miss 30â50% of defects.

lessons.title: IPC-A-610 Standards Overview
lessons.body: IPC-A-610 is the global bible for accepting or rejecting electronic assemblies. It's written by IPC, a trade association, and it defines what a 'good' solder joint looks like. You don't need to memorize the whole book (it's 400+ pages). But you need to know three classes. Class 1 is for general productsâtoys, cheap radios. Class 2 is for dedicated serviceâTVs, computers, phones. Class 3 is for high-reliabilityâmedical, aerospace, military. Most African workshops build Class 2 products. For Class 2, a solder joint must be smooth, shiny, and have a concave fillet (like a tiny volcano). The solder must wet the pad and the lead. No cracks, no voids, no bridges. For through-hole, solder should fill the hole and form a fillet on both sides. For surface-mount, the fillet must be visible on all sides of the component. IPC-A-610 gives specific numbers: for example, a solder fillet on a chip resistor should be at least 0.2 mm high. A void in a BGA solder ball is acceptable if it's less than 25% of the ball's area. You can download a free summary of IPC-A-610 from the IPC website. Print the key pages and laminate them for your workbench. Train your inspectors using the 'accept' and 'reject' photos in the standard. In Africa, many buyers (like those exporting to Europe) require IPC-A-610 Class 2 compliance. If you can show you inspect to this standard, you can charge 20â30% more. Start by buying a used copy of IPC-A-610 from eBay or Amazon; it costs $50â$100. Or find a local training center that offers IPC certificationâit's worth the investment.

lessons.title: Solder Joint Inspection
lessons.body: Solder joint inspection is the heart of quality control. A good solder joint looks like a shiny, smooth fillet that curves like a tiny volcano from the pad up to the component lead. It should be concave, not convex. A convex blob means too much solder. A dull, grainy joint means cold solderâthe iron wasn't hot enough or you moved the joint while it cooled. Cold joints crack easily and cause intermittent faults. Inspect each joint under 10x magnification. Use a pointed probe (like a dental pick) to gently push on the joint. If it moves, it's a cold jointâreject it. For through-hole joints, check that solder wicks up the lead and fills the hole. A good joint has a fillet on both the top and bottom of the board. For surface-mount, check for 'tombstoning'âwhere one end of a chip component lifts off the pad. That happens when one pad heats faster than the other. Also check for 'solder balls'âtiny spheres of solder that can roll around and cause shorts. Remove them with tweezers. For fine-pitch ICs, use a microscope. Look for bridges between pins. A bridge is any solder connecting two adjacent pins. Even a hair-thin bridge will short the circuit. Use solder wick and flux to remove bridges. For BGA (ball grid array) packages, you can't see the joints. You need X-ray inspection, which is expensive. Instead, do a 'dye and pry' test on a sample: inject dye under the chip, let it cure, then pry it off. The dye shows where solder didn't wet. In a small African workshop, focus on visual inspection of visible joints. Keep a log of every defect type you find. After 100 boards, you'll see patternsâmaybe your iron temperature is too low, or your flux is expired. Fix the process, not just the board.

lessons.title: Documenting Inspection Results
lessons.body: If you don't write it down, it didn't happen. Documentation is your proof of quality and your tool for improvement. Start with a simple paper log. For each board, record: serial number, date, inspector name, and a list of defects found. Use a checklist with common defect codes: 'SB' for solder bridge, 'CJ' for cold joint, 'MP' for missing part, 'WP' for wrong part, 'TO' for tombstone, 'SC' for scratch. For each defect, note the reference designator (e.g., R12, C5) and the location. Take a photo with your phoneâmost phones have a 12 MP camera that's good enough for documentation. Store photos in a folder named by board serial number. At the end of each day, count the defects. Calculate your first-pass yield: (number of boards with zero defects / total boards inspected) Ã 100. A good target for hand assembly is 90% first-pass yield. If you're below 80%, you have a process problem. Use a simple spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Excel) to track defects over time. Make a Pareto chart: which defect type is most common? If 60% of your defects are solder bridges, train your assemblers on drag soldering or use a smaller solder tip. For customer orders, include a 'Certificate of Conformance' that states you inspected to IPC-A-610 Class 2 and list the serial numbers. This builds trust. In Africa, where buyers may be overseas, clear documentation can be the difference between getting repeat orders or not. Keep records for at least 2 years. If a customer reports a failure, you can trace it back to the exact board and inspector. That's how you learn and improve.

lessons.title: Quality Control Tools and Techniques
lessons.body: Quality control is not just inspectionâit's a system. Start with the 'Plan-Do-Check-Act' cycle. Plan: set a quality target (e.g., 95% first-pass yield). Do: assemble boards. Check: inspect and record defects. Act: fix the root cause. For root cause analysis, use the '5 Whys' method. Ask 'why' five times. Example: Why did the board fail? A solder bridge. Why? Too much solder. Why? The iron tip was too large. Why? We didn't have the right tip. Why? We never ordered it. So the fix is to order the correct tip. Other tools: a 'fishbone diagram' (also called Ishikawa) helps you brainstorm causes. Draw a spine and branches for Man, Machine, Material, Method, Measurement, and Environment. For electronics, common causes are: wrong iron temperature (Method), expired flux (Material), humid air (Environment), or uncalibrated multimeter (Measurement). Use a multimeter to check for shorts and opens. A cheap $20 multimeter is fine. For continuity, set it to beep mode. For voltage, set to DC 20V. For current, use a bench power supply with current limiting. Also use a 'test jig'âa simple board with pogo pins that connects to your board's test points. This speeds up functional testing. In Africa, you can make a test jig from a wooden block, pogo pins (from AliExpress), and a multimeter. Finally, do 'sampling inspection'âinspect every 5th board fully, but do a quick visual on all. That balances speed and quality. Train everyone on these tools. Post the Pareto chart on the wall. Celebrate when you hit your target. Quality is a habit, not an accident.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Inspection and Quality Control for Electronics Assembly

In African electronics assembly operations â from contract manufacturers in Lagos and Nairobi to solar inverter assemblers in Accra and Johannesburg â inspection is not a bureaucratic afterthought. It is the gate that decides whether a batch ships, gets reworked, or becomes warranty cost. For an SME running a small SMT line or hand-assembly bench, a disciplined inspection routine protects cash flow, customer relationships, and the ability to win the next order.

This lesson is a practical reference you can pin to the wall of your inspection station. It covers what to look for, how to look for it, the standards that define acceptable work, and the tools that make quality measurable rather than a matter of opinion.

Visual Inspection Criteria

Visual inspection is the first and cheapest line of defence. At a minimum, every assembled board should pass a structured check covering: correct component orientation and value, no missing or extra parts, no tombstoning or billboarding, no solder bridges, no disturbed joints, clean flux residue within limits, and no physical damage to pads, traces, or connectors. In African workshops where reflow ovens may be older or hand-soldering is common, the two most frequent defects are insufficient solder and cold joints â both visible under good light.

Inspection must be done against a written standard, not against the inspector's mood. The reference for most commercial work is IPC-A-610, which defines three classes: Class 1 (general electronics), Class 2 (dedicated service, the default for most African contract work), and Class 3 (high reliability â medical, aerospace, automotive safety). Know which class your customer is paying for before you start rejecting boards.

Using Magnification and Lighting

Human visual acuity limits reliable inspection to features around 0.2 mm without aid. For 0402 chip components, fine-pitch QFN, or BGA perimeter inspection, you need 3Ã to 10Ã magnification. A stereo microscope with 10Ãâ40Ã is the workshop standard; a 5Ã loupe is acceptable for coarse through-hole work but not for fine pitch.

Lighting matters as much as magnification. Use diffuse, shadow-free illumination from at least two angles. Ring lights are common but can hide fillet shape; a combination of ring and oblique light reveals both presence and profile of solder. Avoid single-point LED torches â they create glare that hides cold joints. In dusty or humid environments (common in coastal West Africa and East African industrial parks), keep lenses capped and clean them with lint-free wipes before each shift.

IPC-A-610 Standards Overview

IPC-A-610 is the most widely used workmanship standard in the world and is the de facto requirement for most export-bound African electronics. It is a visual acceptance document â it tells you what a joint, a component placement, or a PCB surface should look like, not how to achieve it. Key sections cover soldering (through-hole and SMT), component mounting, mechanical assembly, and cleanliness.

For an SME, the practical move is to buy or borrow the current revision, extract the criteria relevant to your product family, and build a one-page acceptance sheet per product. This turns a 400-page standard into a usable shop-floor tool. Training on IPC-A-610 is available through IPC-certified centres, and some African technical universities and industry associations now offer short courses.

Solder Joint Inspection

A good solder joint has a smooth, shiny, concave fillet that wets both the pad and the lead. The wetting angle should be low â solder should flow onto the surfaces, not ball up. For lead-free solder (now standard in most export work due to RoHS), the surface is slightly matte but should still be smooth and continuous; do not confuse this with a cold joint, which is rough, dull, and lumpy.

Common defects and their causes:

  • Insufficient solder: too little paste, poor stencil aperture, or short reflow. Reject if the fillet does not cover the pad.
  • Excess solder: too much paste or poor pad design. Acceptable only if it does not hide the lead or bridge to a neighbour.
  • Cold joint: insufficient heat or contaminated surface. Dull, grainy, and unreliable â always reject.
  • Bridging: excess paste or poor stencil release. Always reject; it causes shorts.
  • Disturbed joint: movement during cooling. Frosty appearance â reject.
  • Lifted pad or cracked fillet: thermal stress or handling damage â reject and investigate process.

Documenting Inspection Results

Documentation is what converts inspection from a cost into a business asset. Without records, you cannot prove conformance to a customer, cannot trace a field failure back to a batch, and cannot see which defect keeps recurring. At minimum, record: date, batch/lot number, inspector name, product and revision, inspection class, defects found (type, location, quantity), disposition (accept, rework, scrap), and rework actions taken.

Photograph every defect. A phone camera with a cheap macro clip-on lens is enough. Store images by batch number. When a customer complains six months later, you can show exactly what left your facility and what your process was. This is also the evidence base for continuous improvement â Pareto your defect types monthly.

Table 1: Defect frequency observed in SME electronics assembly (illustrative, based on industry inspection data)

Insufficient solder~25%Stencil aperture / paste volumeVisual, 5â10Ã
Solder bridge~20%Paste excess, stencil releaseVisual, 5â10Ã
Cold / disturbed joint~18%Reflow profile, handlingVisual, oblique light
Component misalignment~15%Placement accuracy, vibrationVisual, AOI if available
Tombstoning~10%Uneven pad heatingVisual, 10Ã
Missing / wrong component~7%Feeder error, kit errorVisual + BOM check
Pad / trace damage~5%Handling, reworkVisual, 10Ã

Source: compiled from IPC defect trend reports and SME assembly line observations; percentages are indicative and vary by product mix.

Quality Control Tools and Techniques

Inspection alone does not create quality â it detects it. The tools below are the ones that make sense for an African SME without a full metrology lab.

  • First Article Inspection (FAI): fully inspect the first board of a new batch or after any process change. Do not release the batch until FAI passes.
  • In-Process Checks: inspect after paste printing (paste height/volume), after placement (orientation), and after reflow (joints). Catching defects early is far cheaper than at final test.
  • Statistical Process Control (SPC): track defect rate per batch on a simple chart. If it trends up, stop and investigate before shipping.
  • Pareto Analysis: rank defect types monthly. Attack the top one or two â this is where most of your rework cost sits.
  • 5 Whys / Root Cause: for every recurring defect, ask why five times. Fix the process, not the symptom.
  • Calibration: verify your microscope, light source, and any measurement tools on a schedule. An uncalibrated tool gives false confidence.
  • Supplier Quality: inspect incoming PCBs and components. A bad batch of boards from a cheap supplier will cost you more in rework than you saved.
Table 2: Inspection stage, tool, and acceptance reference by product class

Reflow jointsVisual, oblique lightSpot check100% visual100% + X-ray for BGA
CleaningVisual, ionic testVisualVisualIonic contamination test

Source: IPC-A-610 acceptability classes and IPC-J-STD-001 process requirements (IPC International).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Lead and Flux Exposure

Solder wire, paste, and flux fumes are hazardous. Lead-containing solder (still used in some repair and legacy work) can be absorbed through skin and ingested. Flux fumes irritate airways. In African workshops with limited ventilation, this is a real occupational health risk.

  • Always solder and inspect under fume extraction or with an open window and fan moving air away from your face.
  • Wear nitrile gloves when handling solder paste and leaded wire. Do not eat, drink, or smoke at the bench.
  • Wash hands with soap after every shift, before eating or touching your face.
  • Store solder paste and flux in sealed containers; label them clearly.
  • Dispose of solder dross and used wipes as hazardous waste, not in general rubbish.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm the inspection class (1, 2, or 3) and the customer's acceptance standard before starting.
  2. Verify magnification (3â10Ã minimum for SMT) and diffuse, shadow-free lighting.
  3. Check component orientation, value, and placement against the BOM and assembly drawing.
  4. Inspect every solder joint for concave fillet, wetting, and absence of bridges or cold joints.
  5. Check for physical damage: lifted pads, cracked traces, damaged connectors, contamination.
  6. Record every defect with type, location, quantity, and a photograph.
  7. Disposition each board: accept, rework with instructions, or scrap. Never ship an unresolved reject.
  8. Review defect trends weekly; act on the top cause before it repeats in the next batch.

Further Reading

  • IPC-A-610 Table of Contents (IPC International) â official overview of the acceptability standard and its classes.
  • IPC-A-610 product page â current revision, training, and certification information.
  • IPC J-STD-001 â soldering process requirements that sit alongside IPC-A-610.
  • IPC/WHMA-A-620 â cable and wire harness acceptability, useful for assemblers building looms.
  • OSHA Lead Safety Guidance â free occupational safety reference for lead exposure in electronics work.

Business takeaway: Inspection is not a cost centre â it is the mechanism that protects your margin. Every defect caught at the bench is a defect that does not become a return, a refund, or a lost customer. For African electronics SMEs competing for export and industrial contracts, a documented, standards-based inspection routine is often the difference between being taken seriously and being treated as a low-cost gamble.

quiz.q: What is the recommended magnification for inspecting solder joints on a typical circuit board?
quiz.explanation: 10x magnification is sufficient to see most solder joint defects like cold joints and bridges.

quiz.q: Which lighting technique makes shiny solder look bright and dull solder look dark?
quiz.explanation: Coaxial lighting directs light along the viewing axis, enhancing contrast between shiny and dull surfaces.

quiz.q: What does IPC-A-610 Class 2 apply to?
options: B) Dedicated service products like computers
C) High-reliability products like medical devices
quiz.explanation: Class 2 is for dedicated service electronics, which includes most consumer and industrial products.

quiz.q: What is a 'cold solder joint'?
options: A) A joint made with lead-free solder
B) A joint that looks dull and grainy
C) A joint that is too shiny
D) A joint with too much solder
quiz.explanation: Cold joints appear dull and grainy due to improper heating or movement during cooling.

quiz.q: What defect is described as one end of a chip component lifting off the pad?
quiz.explanation: Tombstoning occurs when uneven heating causes one end of a component to lift.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing a solder bridge between two IC pins?
quiz.explanation: Solder wick with flux effectively removes excess solder without damaging the board.

quiz.q: What is the first-pass yield if 18 out of 20 boards have zero defects?
quiz.explanation: First-pass yield = (18/20) Ã 100 = 90%.

quiz.q: Which defect code might you use for a missing component?
quiz.explanation: MP stands for 'missing part', a common defect code.

quiz.q: What is the '5 Whys' technique used for?
quiz.explanation: The 5 Whys is a root cause analysis method to find the underlying cause of a problem.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a common cause of solder bridges?
quiz.explanation: Correct iron temperature reduces bridges; the others increase the risk.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a solder ball on a board?
options: A) Ignore it if it's small
C) Push it under a component
quiz.explanation: Solder balls can cause shorts and must be removed.

quiz.q: What is a 'Certificate of Conformance' used for?
options: A) To certify the inspector's training
B) To prove the product meets a standard
C) To list all components used
D) To show the board's serial number
quiz.explanation: A Certificate of Conformance states that the product was inspected to a specific standard.

quiz.q: Which class of IPC-A-610 is for high-reliability products like medical devices?
quiz.explanation: Class 3 covers high-reliability electronics where failure is not an option.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a test jig with pogo pins?
options: A) To hold the board during soldering
B) To speed up functional testing
quiz.explanation: A test jig with pogo pins allows quick connection to test points for functional testing.

quiz.q: What does a fishbone diagram help with?
options: B) Brainstorming causes of a problem
quiz.explanation: A fishbone diagram organizes potential causes of a problem into categories.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a good solder joint?
quiz.explanation: A concave fillet indicates proper wetting and solder amount.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean microscope lenses?
quiz.explanation: Microfiber cloths clean lenses without scratching.

quiz.q: What is the acceptable void percentage in a BGA solder ball for Class 2?
quiz.explanation: IPC-A-610 Class 2 allows voids up to 25% of the ball's area.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for 'dye and pry' testing of BGA joints?
options: B) Dye and a pry tool
quiz.explanation: Dye and pry is a destructive test to inspect BGA joints without X-ray.

quiz.q: What is the first step in visual inspection?
quiz.explanation: Start by comparing the board to the BOM for missing parts.

quiz.q: What does a 'cold joint' look like?
quiz.explanation: Cold joints are dull and grainy due to poor heating.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common defect in through-hole soldering?
quiz.explanation: Through-hole defects include bridges and insufficient hole fill.

quiz.q: What is the recommended frequency for full inspection in sampling inspection?
quiz.explanation: Sampling inspection often inspects every 5th board fully while doing quick visual on all.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a scratch that exposes copper?
options: B) Cover it with solder mask
D) Paint it with nail polish
quiz.explanation: Exposed copper will oxidize and cause faults, so the board should be rejected.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a category in a fishbone diagram?
quiz.explanation: The classic 6 Ms are Man, Machine, Material, Method, Measurement, and Environment; Money is not one.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a wrist strap when inspecting boards?
options: A) To keep your hands warm
quiz.explanation: A grounded wrist strap prevents electrostatic discharge from damaging components.

quiz.q: Which IPC-A-610 class is most common for consumer electronics?
quiz.explanation: Class 2 covers dedicated service products like computers and phones.

quiz.q: What is the first-pass yield if 45 out of 50 boards pass inspection?
What should you do before inspecting a board under magnification?
options: B) Calibrate your eyes with a known-good board
quiz.explanation: Calibrating with a known-good board helps you recognize acceptable joints.

quiz.q: Which of these is a root cause analysis tool?
quiz.explanation: 5 Whys is a root cause analysis technique.
